title: Disaggregated Storage and Compute: How Modern Cloud Databases Decoupled the Storage Engine and Made 'The Log the Database'
summary: Traditional relational databases like PostgreSQL and MySQL couple SQL execution, query planning, and disk page management inside a single virtual machine. When scaling read traffic or recovering from a crash, the engine must write entire 8KB or 16KB dirty data pages to disk and replicate complete database snapshots across replicas, causing massive I/O bottlenecks and multi-minute failovers. Cloud-native databases like Amazon Aurora and Neon rearchitect this relationship by turning 'the log into the database.' Instead of writing modified data pages over network-attached block devices, compute instances only ship compact write-ahead log (WAL) records to a multi-tenant, distributed storage fleet. Dedicated storage nodes asynchronously apply the log records to construct pages on-demand, execute six-way replication across three availability zones, and enable sub-second read-replica provisioning without moving a single gigabyte of storage.
analogyTitle: The Real-Life Analogy: The Single Master Chef Running to the Mill vs. The Executive Kitchen with an Automated Pantry Fleet
analogy:
Imagine a high-end restaurant with a master chef preparing meals.

Under a Coupled Monolithic Architecture (The All-In-One Chef), the chef not only takes customer orders and sautés food, but whenever a batch of bread is needed, the chef leaves the stove, runs out to the backyard mill to grind wheat, kneads raw dough, loads it into an oven, and sweeps the floor (writing entire 8KB dirty pages to disk). If the restaurant gets busy, adding another chef requires buying an entire second building with an identical duplicate wheat field, mill, and oven (full replica storage cloning). If the oven breaks, the chef spends an hour scrubbing and rebuilding it before cooking again (crash recovery redo-logging).

Under a Disaggregated Storage Architecture (The Executive Kitchen & Automated Pantry), the chef never touches raw grain or sweeps floors. The chef only writes short, standardized ingredient tickets: 'add 2 eggs, 50g flour' (compact WAL records) and sends them down a pneumatic tube to an underground automated pantry facility. The pantry fleet runs 24/7, handles all storage, bakes the bread in parallel, and instantly slides warm loaves up to the counter when requested. Adding five new cooking stations takes 30 seconds because all chefs share the exact same automated pantry without duplicating a single storage room.

sections.heading: 1. The Monolithic Bottleneck: Why Dirty Page Flushing Chokes Relational Databases
sections.content:
In traditional relational database systems (PostgreSQL and MySQL), the database engine runs directly on top of a local disk or a network-attached block device (such as AWS EBS):

• The Buffer Pool and Dirty Page Writes: When a transaction executes an UPDATE, the database does not write modified bytes directly to disk. It alters an in-memory representation of an 8KB page (PostgreSQL) or 16KB page (MySQL) in the shared buffer pool, marking the page as 'dirty'. To prevent data loss, the engine writes a small record to the Write-Ahead Log (WAL) and eventually writes the entire dirty page to disk during checkpointing.
• The I/O Amplification Problem: If an application modifies a single 4-byte integer in a row, the database still writes the entire 8KB or 16KB page to disk. To prevent torn pages from hardware crashes during a write, MySQL writes the page twice via its doublewrite buffer. In high-concurrency workloads, over 90% of disk I/O bandwidth is wasted writing redundant page structures rather than actual application payload data.
• Replica Bloat and Sluggish Failover: Traditional read replicas maintain their own private disks. To stay synchronized, they either replay WAL logs against their own local buffer pools or pull raw binary snapshots. Provisioning a new replica requires copying gigabytes or terabytes of physical storage over the network, making autoscaling sluggish and failover unpredictable.

sections.heading: 2. 'The Log is the Database': Moving Write-Ahead Logging to the Storage Fleet
sections.content:
Modern cloud-native databases (such as Amazon Aurora and Neon) break this monolithic coupling by separating compute from storage across a fast network fabric:

• Stateless Compute Instances: The primary database node retains the SQL parser, query planner, and buffer cache, but completely eliminates local persistent disk storage. When transactions commit, the compute node does not flush dirty pages. It generates an append-only stream of fine-grained WAL redo-log records and transmits them across a high-speed network to dedicated storage nodes.
• Storage Nodes with Built-In Log Processing: In traditional setups, storage is passive block storage. In a disaggregated system, storage nodes are active intelligent microservices. Storage nodes receive WAL log records, persist them immediately to NVMe drives, and acknowledge the write. In the background, storage workers coalesce log records against older page snapshots to reconstruct base pages on-demand.
• Eliminating Crash Recovery Delays: In a monolithic database, crashing requires scanning the WAL on disk from the last checkpoint forward, which can take minutes or hours. In disaggregated storage, page reconstruction happens continuously inside the storage fleet. If the compute node crashes, a replacement compute instance boots up in sub-seconds and starts answering queries immediately because database pages are already up-to-date in storage.

sections.heading: 3. Quorum Writes, Sub-Second Read Replicas, and Instant Autoscaling
sections.content:
By offloading durability and state management to the network, disaggregated architectures achieve resilience and elasticity impossible in legacy architectures:

• Quorum Replication Across Availability Zones: Instead of complex two-phase commit protocols, systems like Aurora split the database into 10GB segments and replicate each segment six ways across three availability zones (2 copies per AZ). Writes succeed as soon as 4 of the 6 nodes acknowledge receipt (write quorum). The system survives the complete loss of an entire availability zone plus an additional storage node without losing a single transaction or dropping write availability.
• Zero-Copy Read Replicas: Because database state lives in the shared storage cluster, read replicas do not require private disk volumes. Up to 15 read replicas can mount the identical storage fleet. Replicas process read-only queries from their local buffer pools while receiving lightweight WAL stream updates from the primary to invalidate modified cache lines. Provisioning a new replica takes seconds, not hours.
• Instant Branching and Serverless Sleep: Modern open-source platforms like Neon take disaggregation further by separating storage into Pageservers and Safekeepers. Safekeepers handle quorum WAL writes, while Pageservers materialise historical page versions. This enables git-like instant database branching in milliseconds with copy-on-write semantics and allows idle databases to scale down to zero compute cost instantly.

takeaway: Coupling compute and storage locks relational databases into rigid, high-latency disk bottlenecks. By offloading write-ahead log replay, crash recovery, and multi-AZ quorum replication into a dedicated, distributed storage fleet, disaggregated databases eliminate dirty page flushes, protect against torn page writes, and enable near-instantaneous replica scaling with zero storage duplication.
